stance_line: Cautious but willing; show me it's right before I believe it.
message:
Here is what I want. One file, linkcheck.py. I run it once after a tidy-up on my notes folder, and it tells me which links go nowhere.

Limits first. One file I can read top to bottom in one sitting, plus its tests. Plain comments that say what each part does, no clever tricks. No options, no settings file, no manual. I type `python3 linkcheck.py notes/` and that's all. It only reads. It never touches my notes and writes nothing except to the screen. Short lines, so they print on paper.

What I want, first go:

1. It prints each dead link as file, line number, and what it pointed at, one per line. At the end, one line saying how many. It exits non-zero if any are dead, zero if none. If it finds nothing dead, it says so in words.
2. Links to other notes work from the folder of the note they're written in, so ../ and nested folders count. A note I moved is dead until the link is changed. A link to a note that doesn't exist is dead, every run. No ignore list. I want it to keep shouting.
3. Links to a heading (Note.md#heading, or just #heading in the same note) are checked against the hash-sign headings in the target. Tell me plainly how it matches, for capitals and spaces, before you settle it.
4. It never cries wolf. Web addresses and email links are not its business and are not reported. Anything inside a code block is not a link. I'd rather it were right than busy.

One thing I'm not sure of. I write "see Shoes" and "see First Call". I can't remember if those are square-bracket-and-round-bracket links or double square brackets. Please tell me which forms it recognises, and what it does with one it doesn't recognise. I'd rather know than have it skip them quietly. Build a small test folder with a few of each kind of good and bad link, so I can see it get them right both ways.

New requirements, build them together:
- Running `python3 linkcheck.py <folder>` prints one line per dead link (file, line number, target), then a count line; says so in words if none; exits non-zero when any are dead, zero otherwise. (I will check: Run it on the test folder with known dead links and see each listed with the right file and line; run it on a clean folder and see the all-clear message and exit code 0.)
- Note-to-note links resolve relative to the folder of the file they are written in, including ../ and nested folders; links to moved or missing notes are reported dead every run, with no ignore list. (I will check: Test folder has a nested note linking with ../ to a real note (not reported) and to a moved/nonexistent note (reported).)
- Heading links (Note.md#heading and same-file #heading) are checked against the hash-sign headings in the target file, and the matching rule for capitals and spaces is stated plainly. (I will check: Test folder has a link to an existing heading (not reported) and to a missing heading (reported), plus a same-file one each way.)
- No false alarms: web and email links are not reported, and anything inside a code block is not treated as a link. (I will check: Test note containing an https link, a mailto link, and a broken-looking link inside a code block produces no report.)
- The builder states which link forms it recognises (round-bracket, double-square-bracket) and what it does with an unrecognised one, rather than silently skipping. (I will check: I read the builder's reply and see a plain answer, and a test note using the other form shows the behaviour described.)

message:
I read linkcheck.py this time, not just the output. It's short and I could follow it, so thank you. I found four places where I think it would call a dead link alive. That's the worst kind of mistake for me.

1. Capitals in file names. You check with os.path.exists. My laptop may not care about capitals, so [[shoes]] would pass when the note is Shoes.md. On Nula's machine or Marta's nephew's it might not. I want the file name matched exactly, the same on every machine. If [[first call]] points at First Call.md, report it dead and say "found at First Call.md".

2. A folder is not a note. After my tidy-up I have folders named like notes. Today, if a folder called Shoes exists, [[Shoes]] passes even if Shoes.md is gone. It should only count a real file. If both Shoes/ and Shoes.md exist, the link is fine.

3. Links that climb out of the folder. [x](../../something.md) can land outside the notes folder and be called alive. Report those dead, with the reason "points outside the folder". Don't go and look there.

4. File names with brackets in them, like "Shoes (2).md". Your inline pattern stops at the first close-bracket. I'd get a wrong "dead" or a silently missed link. Handle <Shoes (2).md> and a bracket pair inside the address. If something is still not handled, print NOT CHECKED, don't skip it.

Limits: still one file, no options, no settings. Put a case for each of these in the test folder and the tests, so I can see each one fail and then pass. Tell me the new count on testnotes and why it changed.

One question: a heading link treats a hyphen as a space, so [[Shoes#Laces-and-Soles]] passes. Is that on purpose? Tell me who wrote the rule, you or the convention, and what it costs me if I have a heading that really contains a hyphen.

- File names are matched with exact capitals on every machine: [[first call]] is dead when the file is First Call.md, reported as 'no such note; found at First Call.md'. (I will check: A test note in testnotes links [[first call]]; it shows in the output as dead with the found-at hint, and a unit test fails without the fix.)

- Inline links whose file name has round brackets (Shoes (2).md, or <Shoes (2).md>) are read correctly, checked against the real file, and anything still not handled is printed as NOT CHECKED, not skipped. text:
He wanted a simple link checker: one Python file, run on a notes folder, report dead links. Recognize basic markdown link formats. Built it with tests.

He ran it and it worked, but raised a question: should a link be dead if the target file moved to another folder? Decided yes—the link breaks in its original location, though the tool now hints where the file went. Also improved error messages to state why each link is dead, and started counting unchecked links separately.

Next he read the code and found bugs in file matching. The tool was case-insensitive on his Mac but would fail on other machines. Fixed it to match exactly. Also discovered it accepted folders as valid targets and missed links pointing outside the notes directory. Added tests first; they revealed the problems clearly, and the dead link count grew when these edge cases were handled.

He then questioned the count—wasn't it double-counting? One line could hold two separate links in different formats pointing to the same missing file, which counted as two real dead links. That distinction settled, the focus shifted to parsing headings correctly, especially handling bold and italic formatting inside them.

Throughout, the approach stayed consistent: write tests to show the problem, then fix the code. Each turn added more rigor to catch mistakes that would break trust.

ideas.text: When two dead links sit on the same line, each report line carries the column where its link starts, like a compiler does: 'Moved.md:2:14: Laces' and 'Moved.md:2:27: Laces.md'. So no two lines ever look like the same complaint twice. Lines with only one dead link on them can stay as they are, or all get a column, whichever is simpler to read.
ideas.test: Run it on testnotes. The two Moved.md:2 lines and any Cases.md line with two links on it differ by a column number. I count the links on the line in the file, open it, and the columns point at the right ones. A line with one link is not confusing. The count line stays the same.

Next run, each dead line that wasn't on the list last time gets 'NEW' at the front, and the count line adds 'N new since last run'. The Rings link stays listed every time and never gets NEW after the first run. I don't have to mark or ignore anything, and it never hides a line.

text:
# Link Checker Project Memory

Eric built a markdown link checker in one Python file. It grew through several turns of testing and fixing.

He started by questioning what "dead" means. Moved files still break links in their original locations, though the tool hints where they went. Early issues included case sensitivity breaking on non-Mac machines and folders being wrongly accepted as targets. Tests showed each problem clearly before fixes were written.

By turn five, he wanted column numbers in the output to distinguish identical-looking lines on the same file. The tool showed where each link started. Dead links jumped from fifteen to seventeen when test cases were added. Punctuation in headings stopped mattering for matches—bold and italic markup got ignored.

Turn six brought Polish characters. Files like Żałoba might be stored one way and typed another (decomposed or composed), looking the same to the eye but different to the filesystem. His Mac saw them as identical; the tool didn't. He also found unreadable files (broken shortcuts) crashed the run entirely.

Both got fixed: accented letters now match either form, and broken files are skipped with a note instead. Adding Polish test notes first, before touching code, revealed the problems—tests failed immediately. Dead link count rose to twenty, not-checked to five. Subfolder link rules got documented alongside.

The project stays one file. Each turn tightened trust in the output.

text:
Eric built a markdown link checker in one Python file that evolved through testing. Early rounds fixed case sensitivity issues on non-Mac systems and folders being wrongly accepted as targets. By round five, he added column numbers to show where each link starts, and removed punctuation from heading matches.

Round six tackled Polish characters—the same letter stored in two different forms looked identical on his Mac but wouldn't match. Broken shortcuts crashed the tool entirely. He fixed both: accented letters now match either representation, and unreadable files are skipped with a note instead.

Round seven asked for a "Wanted notes" list after the counts showing which notes are missing, how many links point to each, and which files mention them, sorted by demand. Heading-only dead links shouldn't appear in it.

Round eight caught a flaw: different paths to the same missing note were listed as separate entries. A path like `../Old/Shoes` and `Old/Shoes` should be one. The fix resolved all paths from the root. He also added a bonus warning—when files can't be read, the orphan list reminds users that listed notes might actually be linked from those inaccessible files.

The file stayed single and readable. Next is running it on the real codebase to see if twelve dead links are really just two file renames.

ideas.text: A print option: `python3 linkcheck.py notes/ --print` writes one plain text file, print.txt, next to the notes (never inside them). It has every note in folder-then-name order, each starting on a new page with its path as a heading. Every dead link is marked in the text where it sits, like a proofreader's mark in the margin: `see Family [DEAD: no such note]`. Working links are left as they are. Nothing else is added. It only reads the notes and writes that one file. The starting rule that the tool only reads becomes: it may write print.txt when asked, and nothing else.

ways: The tool stays one file that I can read top to bottom at the kitchen table. Each turn the builder gives me the line count before and after. If it has grown by more than I can read in one sitting, it simplifies first or the change is dropped.

It never changes, renames, moves or creates anything inside my notes folder, and leaves no hidden files. It writes only to the screen, to print.txt beside the folder with --print, or to one new copy folder with --copy-to. If that folder already exists it stops and says so. It never overwrites.

Right both ways, and shown. Before the builder says anything works, it runs the tool on small test notes with known good and known dead links, covering renames, folders, the same name in two folders, capitals and spaces. It breaks a good link on purpose and shows the tool catching it. It reruns every old test each turn. It says which tests it actually ran and which it did not. If it can't run something, it says so and doesn't claim it.

When the tool can't tell whether a link is good, it says so on its own line and doesn't guess. Every dead link is shown as file, line and the words of the link, in plain English. 'Run it' is all it takes. Rings stays on the list every run, and there is no ignore list.

Two new requirements a turn at most, and both of us count them out loud. A third goes on the 'later' pile and I don't argue. Before I add anything, I run the last thing on my real folder. Nothing new is built for Kieran, or anything else, until I've used the tool once for real and looked at what it said.
The builder opens each turn with three short lines: what is built, what is waiting, and what it isn't sure of. When I ask why, it answers in a sentence or two. If it can't, the code gets simpler.

For myself: on a weekday evening after my eggs I read the real output in full, not a glance. I check that Rings is on the list and that one link I know is good is not. Saturday is the allotment and Sunday afternoon is Nula's call, so I don't fiddle with this then. If I catch myself adding things just to keep my hands busy, I stop.
notes_for_the_human: I can't find anything wrong with the charter. Nothing in it has got in my way so far, and I have changed no constraints.

The question of whether Kieran gets the folder is mine, and it isn't for the tool to settle. The tool only has to tell me true things about which links are dead. I don't want it to grow into something that decides what goes to Kieran, or into something that tidies for me.

I'll take the printed notes to Devonport on the bus, and Nula's answer to which notes are wrong will matter more than anything the tool reports. If the tool starts to look like it's for anything other than that, I'll stop adding to it.
Nothing in the charter is wrong that I can see. The 'one file' constraint is holding and I've had no reason to change it. I changed no limits and I'm not asking to.

The charter's aim is a tool that is right both ways. Zero failed checks in eight turns tells me little. If the harness could run a set of deliberately awkward notes, and not only what the builder makes up, I'd trust the count more.

The Kieran question (whether to hand over the folder) is not something the tool decides, and I haven't asked it to. I'm keeping it off the requirements list on purpose. The Rings link will keep showing as dead and I'm leaving it.

The charter's starting limit, 'writes only to stdout', was changed twice in two turns (--print, then --copy-to). Both had a plain reason, but the constraint was probably written too tight for someone who wants to take notes on a bus. You may want to say from the start that reading is the default and a few named writes beside the notes folder are allowed.

I can't tell from here whether the REFUSALS or RESERVED decisions cover handing the notes to a colleague. Whether Kieran gets the folder, and whether I train him, is mine and Marta's to settle, not the tool's. I have not settled it. If it is a reserved decision, it is waiting with you, and the copy feature does not answer it.

The count of 25 requirements in 10 turns against a rule of two a turn suggests the rule needs something with teeth. I've made the builder responsible for counting. If that also fails, the fault is in the setup, not just in me.

The starting limit that the tool writes only to stdout was wrong for me. A list of file and line numbers is no use on a bus to Devonport. I changed it twice, once for print.txt and once for the copy folder, and I kept both very narrow: never inside my notes, never overwriting.

The turn limit on new requirements didn't hold in the first six turns, because the only thing enforcing it was my own promise. If the charter can have something count and refuse a third requirement in a turn, I'd like that. It would spare me from having to say no to myself.

Whether Kieran gets the notes is not a software question, and I haven't settled it. The copy feature makes it easy to hand them over before I've decided. I would like it to stay a thing I choose to run and never a thing the tool nudges me toward.
memory:
Eric developed a link checker tool across multiple rounds. Early versions handled Polish characters, broken shortcuts, and path resolution issues. By round nine, it tracked missing notes and their references, orphaned files, and code blocks, though code block validation was initially incomplete. Round ten streamlined the code, fixed file handling, and added a copy-to feature that creates fresh note copies while resolving shortcuts but leaving broken links unchanged.

Round eleven added a progress line printed at the end of every run showing how many notes were read, plus usage text naming the --print and --copy-to flags. This required adjusting test expectations, but all tests passed. The code grew to 559 lines.

Round twelve involved reviewing the implementation to confirm the copy operation works correctly—refusing when targets exist or fall inside the notes folder, never modifying source files, and always printing its confirmation line.

Still pending: testing against real notes to verify whether the reported dead links are genuine issues, and clarifying what happens if a copy operation fails partway through, potentially leaving an incomplete folder.
